newsitem.title: USA: IBM stock hits new high, but slips back.
newsitem.headline: IBM stock hits new high, but slips back.

text.p: The stock of International Business Machines Corp. hit an all-time high on Tuesday as investors viewed the company as an increasingly safe technology investment, but slipped back amid a drop in technology stocks.

A confluence of events were fuelling the jump in the stock, including bullish comments by a Goldman Sachs analyst, who started coverge of the computer giant and put the stock on the firm's prestigious recommended and priority lists.

IBM rose as high as $177.125, breaking the previous record of $175.875 in August 1987, before the stock market crash of October 1987. The stock closed $1.75 higher at $173.625 on the New York Stock Exchange, where it was the fifth most active issue on volume of more than 4.5 million shares.
Goldman Sachs analyst Laura Conigliaro has a price target of $200 to $225, driving more investor enthusiasm in the stock, traders said.

"The possibilities for upside are increasing, coming from any one of a number of areas, including key hardware lines, services revenues and gross margin, and a shift in the currency cycle," said Conigliaro in her note to clients.

Analysts said that other factors, including recent weakness in the dollar, a positive meeting with Chairman Louis Gerstner last week and a big publicity windfall as its supercomputer made chess history all helped boost IBM.

About 60 percent of IBM's revenues come from outside the United States, so IBM's results are affected by swings in the dollar's value. In the first quarter, IBM's earnings were hurt by the dollar's rise against other currencies.
Last week, after Gerstner held an upbeat meeting with Wall Street analysts, both Credit Suisse First Boston and Prudential Securities raised their price targets on IBM.

"All the pieces are falling into place," said Ahmet Chopra of Credit Suisse First Boston, who cited IBM as a "featured stock" last week. "You have a couple of catalysts. Gerstner's comments, the dollar is weakening, all these things at once."

On Sunday, IBM scored a major publicity coup after its Deep Blue supercomputer made chess history, defeating world champion Garry Kasparov in a highly publicised match. Its victory garnered heavy media coverage, including the front page of the New York Times.
Analysts said the stock may be close to topping out for the near term, but it appears poised to drive over the $200 level on a pre-split basis.
"This move (in IBM) is extended to the upside," said Gregory Nie, technical analyst at Everen Securities.
The stock has surged from a recent low of $129.25 on April 4 on a series of bullish developments, including surprisingly strong first-quarter earnings, a increased dividend and a stock split.
IBM's new shares from its two-for-one stock split will be distributed to shareholders on May 27.

Also Tuesday, IBM unveiled its new ThinkPad 380 notebook computer series. The "all-in-one" design integrates a hard drive, a floppy drive and a CD-ROM in one unit with a 12.1-inch screen and Pentium microprocessor.
IBM said estimated retail prices for the ThinkPad 380 series start at $2,199 depending on model and configuration.
